query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Intermediate-temperature annealing (700–800°C for 10–30 minutes) applied to a eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies will induce phase-selective recrystallization in the soft lamellae while preserving the hard phase skeleton. This treatment is expected to reduce dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries, thereby mitigating local stress concentrations and microcrack initiation, which in turn improves room-temperature tensile ductility (by roughly >30% compared to the as-cast state) without sacrificing overall strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure with pronounced dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries, limited ductility (~25% elongation in tensile tests), and high strength but brittle failure due to microcracking.
generation.conditions: Annealing at approximately 700–800°C for 10–30 minutes followed by room-temperature tensile testing under quasi-static loading (strain rates ~10^(-3) to 10^(-4) s^(-1)) in air.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of phase-selectively recrystallized soft lamellae embedded in a stable hard phase skeleton
generation.mechanism: Partial recrystallization in the soft phase creates more fully developed subgrain boundaries and introduces new slip systems that alleviate dislocation pile-ups. This homogeneous redistribution of dislocations reduces local stress concentrations, thereby delaying microcrack initiation during deformation while the hard phase continues to carry the applied load.
generation.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, the treated alloy will exhibit a significant improvement in tensile ductility (an increase of over 30% relative to the untreated alloy) while maintaining or slightly increasing tensile strength, with strength levels comparable to or exceeding the ~1.2 GPa true fracture stress observed in the as-cast condition.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that shows limited room-temperature ductility (~25% elongation) and high strength with a propensity for dislocation pile-ups and microcracking.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected within a narrow processing window; annealing significantly below or above 700–800°C or for durations much shorter or longer than 10–30 minutes may result in either insufficient recrystallization or excessive coarsening, which would undermine the balance between ductility and strength.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies suggest phase-selective recrystallization can improve ductility, the exact quantitative changes in tensile properties depend on precise control of annealing conditions and microstructural response, warranting experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of samples of the eutectic high-entropy alloy and subject them to annealing treatments that deviate from the proposed optimal range (e.g., 600°C or 900°C for 10–30 minutes, or 700°C for 5 minutes and 60 minutes). Afterwards, perform room-temperature tensile tests under quasi-static conditions and conduct microstructural analysis via electron microscopy to assess the degree of phase-selective recrystallization.
measurements: Yield strength and fracture strength from tensile tests
Microstructural characterization (degree of recrystallization, lamellar morphology, and dislocation distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit at least a 30% improvement in ductility compared to the as-cast baseline, or if the tensile strength deteriorates significantly (falling below the baseline strength), or if similar improvements are observed with annealing conditions outside the targeted window, then the hypothesis that the intermediate-temperature annealing is uniquely beneficial would be falsified.

The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Due to the fine lamellar microstructure with a large number of fcc-bcc interfaces, the alloy show relatively high flow-stresses, ~1400 MPa under quasi-static loading and in excess of 1800 MPa under dynamic loading. Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials. decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) introduced eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) such as AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with dual-phase lamellar microstructures that combined high strength and reasonable ductility at room temperature. Subsequent investigations (PMC5818523, PMC6353877, PMC6687781) focused on thermomechanical routes—cryogenic rolling, warm-rolling, and optimized annealing—to refine lamella spacings, reduce dislocation pile-ups at interfaces, and enhance strength–ductility synergy. Most recently, phase-selective recrystallization strategies (PMC9365806) have been shown to dramatically improve the ductility of EHEAs by controlling recrystallization in the soft phase while preserving a robust, load-bearing hard phase skeleton. Despite these advances, it remains challenging to suppress microcracking at the hierarchical boundaries and maintain or even increase strength simultaneously.
decision.unsolved: A key gap is that dislocation pile-ups persist at certain internal boundaries under room-temperature tensile loads, creating local stress concentrations that initiate cracks. Achieving a uniform, high-density network of interfaces or subgrains that can effectively redistribute or accommodate dislocations without losing strength remains a central challenge.
decision.lever: A short (e.g., 10–30 min) intermediate-temperature annealing (≈700–800 °C) to induce partial or phase-selective recrystallization in the soft lamellae, while retaining the hard phase skeleton. The resulting microstructure should reduce boundary dislocation pile-ups and thereby mitigate crack initiation while preserving, or even elevating, overall strength. Predicted outcomes include a moderate to significant increase in tensile ductility (e.g., > 30% improvement) at room temperature, with strength comparable to or surpassing the as-cast condition. Room-temperature tensile tests in air under quasi-static loading (strain rates ~10–3–10–4/s) will confirm improved ductility and strength. Prior work on partial recrystallization in EHEAs (e.g., PMC9365806) supports this mechanism. A falsification test would apply the same heat treatment at substantially higher or lower temperatures or for much longer or shorter times, to demonstrate that inappropriate processing leads to excessive coarsening or incomplete boundary stabilization, respectively, which would negate the targeted increase in strength–ductility synergy.
decision.why: Selective recrystallization of the soft lamellae produces more accommodating boundaries for dislocations, limiting local stress concentrations. Preserving the hard lamellae ensures advantageous load-bearing capacity remains intact, meeting the dual requirement to increase ductility without sacrificing overall strength.
